dehydrated_text:
Because God's words were, "If you eat from that fruit, you will surely die." Even though the food fruit wasn't poisonous, God still has a duty to kill Adam and Eve. In the Iliad, gods are vengeful, wrathful, but not this God—Yahweh is different. Instead of being angry at Adam and Eve, he offers them a present.

The question then is why? One possibility is that God himself recognizes his mistake in drawing attention to the fruit. Therefore, it's his fault; this god is capable of self-reflection and forgiveness. Another possibility is that God wanted this outcome all along. The man named his wife Eve because she was the mother of all living, honoring her as a true goddess.

God punishes Adam by making him toil for food, becomes a farmer, and punishes Eve by making childbirth painful, and a serpent by making it slither on the ground. God then throws Adam and Eve out of the garden. He fears they might eat from the tree of life and become like him, so he banishes them.

Most people think this is bad, but you can interpret it as good—God chose us to be creative without living forever because creativity requires death. If you live forever, you're not motivated to make your life meaningful or allow future generations to innovate. God's plan includes making us creative, which is divine.

Adam and Eve have children named Cain and Abel. Cain is a farmer, Abel a shepherd. Cain offers fruit to the Lord, while Abel offers fat portions from his flock. The Lord accepts Abel's offering but not Cain's.
